summary.text: Ice–albedo feedback is a climate feedback in which a change in the area of ice caps, glaciers and sea ice changes how much sunlight a planet reflects, and so its surface temperature.
When warming shrinks the ice, darker water or land absorbs more solar energy, which brings more warming and more melting; cooling grows ice and deepens itself the same way.
Shrinking Arctic sea ice is one of the main reasons the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average since 1979.

items.prompt: A warm summer melts a large patch of polar sea ice, leaving open ocean. What does this do to the warming that follows?

options.label: Speeds it up, as dark water soaks up more sunlight
Slows it down, as the cold meltwater chills the air
Changes nothing, as ice and water reflect equally
Slows it down, as open water reflects more sunlight

items.explain: Ice reflects far more solar energy than open water, so losing it lowers albedo, more energy is absorbed, and warming grows.

items.prompt: A planet cools slightly and its ice sheets start to spread. What does this feedback tend to do next?

options.label: Reverse the cooling into warming
Cancel the cooling out exactly
Deepen the cooling further
Have no effect until ice melts

items.explain: More ice raises albedo, which brings more cooling and makes still more ice likely to form.

items.prompt: Why would losing Arctic sea ice for good in summer matter most for warming?

options.label: Summer storms spread the heat further
The Sun shines strongest then, so lost reflection counts most
Summer ice is thicker, so more ice is lost
Winter ice already absorbs most of the sunlight

items.explain: In the Arctic summer the Sun is most intense, so a missing reflective surface has the greatest impact.

items.prompt: Over seven decades Antarctica as a whole warmed very little, unlike the Arctic. What helps explain the difference?

options.label: Antarctica receives no sunlight at all
Antarctic air has fewer greenhouse gases
The ocean around Antarctica has been cooling
Its thick ice cover has stayed very stable

items.explain: Antarctica's ice cover is highly stable, with the East Antarctic ice sheet rising nearly 4 km above sea level, so little net warming followed.

items.prompt: Climate modellers run a simulation in which Arctic ice cover is held fixed while the world warms. What happens to strong Arctic amplification?

options.label: It grows even stronger
It largely disappears
It moves to the tropics
It stays about the same

items.explain: Models show strong Arctic amplification occurs only when significant sea ice is lost and largely vanishes when ice cover is fixed.

items.prompt: Ice loss in the Arctic and Antarctic from 1992 to 2018 had a warming effect equal to what share of all greenhouse gases emitted then?

options.label: About 1%
About 50%
About 10%
Over 100%

items.explain: The combined ice loss over that period had the same warming impact as 10% of the greenhouse gases emitted.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Ice–albedo feedback is a kind of climate change feedback. In it, a change in how much of a planet is covered by ice caps, glaciers and sea ice changes its albedo and its surface temperature. The key fact is that ice is very reflective. Open water, and every other kind of land cover, sends far less of the Sun's energy back out to space than ice does. The feedback happens on Earth, and it can also happen on exoplanets.

paragraphs.heading: How the loop works
paragraphs.text: The cold high latitudes are where lasting snow, glaciers and ice caps are most likely, sometimes even growing into ice sheets. If the climate warms, the ice shrinks and more open water or bare land is exposed. Albedo drops, more solar energy is absorbed, and that brings more warming and still more loss of reflective ice and snow. The loop also runs the other way: cooling spreads ice, raises albedo, cools things further and makes yet more ice likely.

paragraphs.heading: In Earth's deep past
paragraphs.text: This feedback plays a powerful part in global climate change. It mattered both when Snowball Earth conditions began, nearly 720 million years ago, and when they ended about 630 million years ago, when the thaw likely involved a gradual darkening of the surface by built-up dust. During the Pleistocene, from about 2.6 million to about 10,000 years ago, it was a core factor in the advance and retreat of ice sheets.

paragraphs.heading: The Arctic today
paragraphs.text: Human greenhouse gas emissions have had many effects around the globe, and the decline of Arctic sea ice is one of the most visible. As the sea ice shrinks, it reflects less sunlight. Since 1979, when continuous satellite readings of Arctic sea ice began, the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average, a pattern called Arctic amplification, and lost sea ice is one of the main reasons. In model studies, strong amplification shows up only in months of major ice loss, and it mostly vanishes when the simulated ice cover is held fixed.

paragraphs.heading: Antarctica is different
paragraphs.text: Antarctica behaves differently because its ice cover is very stable. The East Antarctic ice sheet is so thick that its surface stands nearly 4 km above sea level, and the continent has seen very little net warming over the past seven decades, mostly in West Antarctica. Ice loss there is driven mainly by a warming Southern Ocean, which took in 35–43% of all the heat the oceans absorbed between 1970 and 2017.

paragraphs.heading: The global effect
paragraphs.text: Worldwide, the feedback's effect on temperature is smaller but still notable. Arctic sea ice decline from 1979 to 2011 is estimated to have added radiative forcing of 0.21 watts per square meter (W/m²), a quarter of the forcing from rising CO₂ over the same years. Taken together, changes in ice cover between 1992 and 2018 had the same warming effect as 10% of all human greenhouse gas emissions over that time. Lasting loss of ice in the Arctic summer, when the Sun shines most strongly, is estimated to bring about 0.19 °C (0.34 °F) of global warming.

paragraphs.heading: A record low in 2023
paragraphs.text: In 2023 Antarctic sea ice shrank to its smallest extent in 45 years of satellite records. Unusual northward movement of sea ice left wide stretches of open water, which lowered the albedo and set off an ice–albedo loop that sped up melting as more sunlight was absorbed. That year global mean temperature also reached 1.5 K above pre-industrial levels, leaving an unexpected gap of around 0.2 K even after counting human warming and El Niño. That gap was traced to record lows in the planet's albedo, which contributed about 0.22 ± 0.04 K.
